## In one sentence

A species distribution is the geographic pattern of where a species occurs,
produced by environment, movement, history, and interactions.

## Range and occupancy

Range is the geographic extent of a species. Occupancy is whether the species is
present at a defined set of sites. A species can occupy few sites inside a broad
range, and detection may be imperfect: absence from a survey is not always true
absence.

## What shapes a distribution?

Important processes include:

- abiotic suitability, such as temperature, moisture, and soil;
- resource availability and biotic interactions;
- dispersal ability and barriers to movement;
- disturbance and land-use history;
- evolutionary history and past climate.

A distribution model is therefore a hypothesis about which processes limit a
range, not a complete explanation by itself.

## Metapopulations

A metapopulation is a set of local populations linked by dispersal. Local
extinctions can be followed by recolonisation. Connectivity can maintain a
regional population, while isolated habitat patches can increase extinction risk.

::: {.callout-tip}
When mapping a species, record survey effort and detection conditions. Maps of
observations often show where people looked as much as where the species lives.
:::

## Check your understanding

Compare two habitat patches with the same area but different connectivity.
Predict how colonisation and local extinction might differ between them.
